payload.problem_addressed: Long-horizon LLM agents accumulate task-state contamination: unsupported assumptions and outdated plans persist in history and distort subsequent decisions, and prior world models that simulate high-entropy tool observations don't address this.
payload.method_summary: AEWM has two capabilities sharing one model: Action Judge classifies a proposed reasoning-action pair (given history + task) as Critical, Exploratory, or Noisy before execution; for Noisy pairs, State Revision generates a replacement reasoning-action pair grounded in the same history. EditAct integrates both: it keeps critical/exploratory proposals, substitutes revised ones for noisy proposals, executes the selected action in the real environment, and appends the real observation to history. AEWM-RFT then rejection-sample fine-tunes the base agent on verified EditAct trajectories so gains persist without AEWM at inference.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper proposes the Agent-Editing World Model (AEWM), which predicts the downstream effect of an agent's proposed reasoning-action pair and, when that pair is judged noisy, directly edits it using real execution feedback rather than simulating environment observations. EditAct integrates this judge-then-edit loop with real execution across Search, Terminal, and Software-Engineering agent domains, and AEWM-RFT distills the resulting corrected trajectories back into the base agent via rejection-sampling fine-tuning so gains persist without AEWM at inference time.
key_architecture_choices: Pre-execution state s_t = h_t (history) concatenated with the agent's proposed reasoning-action pair, judged before execution
Single model serves both Action Judge (3-way classification: critical/exploratory/noisy) and State Revision (generative repair)
Two-stage training: mid-training on 52B tokens for interaction knowledge, then SFT on 120K curated examples for judgment and revision
EditAct: retains the agent's original action if critical/exploratory, substitutes AEWM's revised action if noisy, then executes in the real environment
AEWM-RFT: rejection-sampling fine-tuning on verified EditAct trajectories to internalize gains without online AEWM guidance at inference
payload.headline_results: AEWM reaches 70.5% macro-F1 on the Action Judge benchmark (10.6 points over the strongest frontier baseline); EditAct improves average scores by 3.2-6.7 points over the strongest baseline across six benchmarks and three agent backbones; AEWM-RFT exceeds Self-RFT by 2.2-2.6 points across three domains without online AEWM guidance.
claimed_advantages: Avoids simulating high-entropy, execution-dependent tool responses that offer limited value once real feedback is available
Directly changes the state underlying subsequent decisions rather than merely providing a critique
Corrected trajectories transfer supervision to the base agent via AEWM-RFT without needing AEWM online at inference
Outperforms agent-resampling and reasoning-hint alternatives, showing direct state editing beats regenerate-and-select
limitations: Gains on Terminal and SWE are limited when paired with a much stronger inference agent (Qwen3.5-Plus), likely due to the capacity gap between AEWM and the agent it edits
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: The State Revision / EditAct mechanism -- judging a proposed decision as noisy and generating a direct replacement using real execution feedback, then continuing from the repaired state -- is a close analog to the repair/edit-distillation technique named in our structural-validity care area: hexgen's best-of-N verifier screening could be extended so that once a sampled program prefix is flagged invalid by the frozen verifier (analogous to 'noisy'), a trained repair model edits the offending block/sweep/projection command(s) rather than discarding the whole rollout, and verified repairs could seed AEWM-RFT-style rejection-sampling fine-tuning to internalize the fix distribution into hexgen's decoder directly.
payload.reviewer_notes: Domain is long-horizon LLM tool-use agents (web search, terminal, software engineering), not geometric/CAD program synthesis -- the transfer is at the mechanism level (judge-then-edit-then-verify), not a reusable component or code. The paper reports diminishing returns when the inference agent is much stronger than AEWM, so a hexgen repair model would likely need to scale/retrain alongside the main decoder. No explicit code URL found in the extracted text (a 'Dataset GitHub' link is referenced but not printed).
payload.implementation_cost_estimate: M -- requires building a separate 'noisy-prefix' judge plus a repair/edit model trained on (broken rollout, verifier feedback, fixed rollout) triples, distinct from the existing best-of-N + frozen-verifier pipeline.
dependencies_on_other_methods: An execution environment that returns real, verifiable feedback (analogous to hexgen's deterministic mesher + verifier)

payload.problem_addressed: In outcome-reward RL for long-horizon tool-use agents, an all-fail group of sampled trajectories yields no training signal, failed attempts can't be distinguished by how close they came to completion, and turns that advance the task get the same credit as turns that don't.
payload.method_summary: ProCredit reruns the task's existing acceptance checks after every turn during training, defines progress as the fraction of checks passed, and rewards each turn by the change in progress between consecutive turns (r_t = c*(Phi_t - Phi_{t-1})). These turn rewards feed both a trajectory-level advantage (GRPO-style, comparing attempts at the same task) and a turn-level advantage (the onward return from each turn), and the policy update sums both advantages within a clipped, token-level policy-gradient objective.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper proposes ProCredit, which converts a long-horizon agentic task's existing binary acceptance checks into a verified, environment-grounded progress signal read after every turn, rather than relying solely on the terminal outcome reward or a learned reward/critic model. This progress signal supplies both a trajectory-level advantage (separating failed attempts by how much they completed) and a turn-level advantage (crediting the specific turn where progress occurred), which the authors show via ablation is what drives the improvement, not merely having any progress signal at all.
key_architecture_choices: Task progress Phi(s) defined as the fraction of the task's existing acceptance checks that pass in state s, read only during training
Turn reward r_t = c*(Phi_t - Phi_{t-1}), the change in progress between consecutive turns
Two-level credit: trajectory-level advantage (GRPO-style, across attempts at the same task) plus turn-level advantage (onward return from each turn), summed in the policy update
Built on a GRPO/LOOP-style clipped, token-level policy-gradient objective, omitting the KL term
payload.headline_results: Starting from Qwen3.5 base models at three scales on AppWorld, ProCredit outperforms outcome-reward and progress-based baselines (GRPO, RLOO, DAPO, SALT, GiGPO) in task completion rate at every scale on both test sets, exceeding the strongest outcome-reward baseline by 4.1 percentage points at 4B; a second environment (ToolSandbox) shows the same direction of improvement, and BFCL function-calling ability does not decline.
claimed_advantages: Uses the task's existing acceptance checks as the intermediate signal, verified in the environment rather than estimated by a learned reward model or critic
Gives all-fail groups nonzero training signal by separating failed attempts by how much they completed
Assigns credit within a trajectory without requiring other trajectories to reach the same state (unlike step-level methods such as GiGPO)
Ablations show the gain specifically comes from crediting progress to the turn where it occurs, not merely adding it to the trajectory score
limitations: Requires task progress to be measurable at intermediate states via rerunnable acceptance checks; with only one or two checks, or all checks passing only on the final turn, the method degenerates to plain GRPO
Gains decrease with model size, since larger models produce fewer all-fail groups and failed attempts
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: hexgen already has a frozen, machine-checkable verifier (compiles, zero inverted elements, quality bounds, surface-match, feature-edge capture) -- ProCredit's core idea transfers directly: rerun a subset of that verifier's checks after each emitted block/sweep/projection command during autoregressive generation to get a fraction-of-checks-passed progress signal, then use the *change* in that fraction between consecutive generation steps as a dense, per-command RL reward. This would let an RL fine-tuning stage over hexgen's decoder credit the specific command that first produces an inverted element or breaks surface-match fidelity, rather than only rewarding/penalizing the whole best-of-N candidate at the end -- directly addressing the 'self-play/verifier-in-the-loop training' care area, and it would make all-fail best-of-N batches (no candidate compiles) still informative during RL fine-tuning, which outcome-only training currently discards.
payload.reviewer_notes: Domain is text/tool-use agentic RL (AppWorld app-automation tasks), not geometric/program-mesh generation, so the transfer is at the mechanism level only. Key caveat from the paper's own discussion: progress must come from the environment state, not from the policy's own predictions, or group normalization lets the policy game the signal without improving task success -- for hexgen this means incremental verifier checks used for reward must run against actual partial program execution/mesh state, not a learned proxy. The method also assumes checks are meaningful on partial/intermediate states; hexgen's verifier currently seems designed to check only completed candidates, so some checks (e.g. inverted-elements-so-far, partial surface coverage) would need engineering to be well-defined mid-generation.
payload.implementation_cost_estimate: M -- requires (a) making a subset of hexgen's verifier checks runnable/meaningful on partial/incomplete programs, and (b) adding a GRPO-style RL fine-tuning stage on top of the current supervised-imitation training to consume the resulting per-step progress rewards.
dependencies_on_other_methods: GRPO-style group-relative policy optimization / LOOP baseline
An environment whose acceptance/verifier checks can be rerun on intermediate (not just terminal) states

provenance.problem_addressed: a group with no successful trajectory yields no training signal, failed attempts cannot be told apart by how close they came to completion
provenance.method_summary: it reruns the acceptance checks after each turn, rewards the turn by its change in progress, and uses these rewards to assign credit both across attempts at the same task and across the turns within a trajectory
provenance.contributions_summary: We propose ProCredit, which turns this verified progress into credit
provenance.headline_results: ProCredit outperforms outcome-reward baselines and progress-based baselines in task completion rate at every scale on both test sets, exceeding the strongest outcome-reward baseline by 4.1 percentage points at 4B
provenance.claimed_advantages: The acceptance checks that decide success can also be run on intermediate states, so progress is as verifiable as the outcome.
provenance.limitations: ProCredit requires task progress to be measurable at intermediate states, which holds whenever the environment state is accessible and the acceptance checks can be rerun.

payload.impact_rationale: If adapted, a noisy-prefix judge plus a repair/edit model could reduce non-compiling/invalid best-of-N candidates by teaching the decoder to fix its own broken rollouts rather than discard them -- a direct lever on the top-priority structural-validity care area. Impact is capped because the technique is demonstrated only in a very different domain (LLM tool-use agents) and would need a from-scratch repair-model and training-data pipeline for hex-meshing programs, with no empirical evidence yet that it transfers to program/geometry generation.
payload.effort_rationale: Requires building a new 'noisy-prefix' classifier and a generative repair model, synthesizing (broken rollout, verifier diagnostic, fixed rollout) training triples for hex-meshing programs, and wiring rejection-sampling fine-tuning around the existing best-of-N plus verifier pipeline -- a substantial new subsystem, not a drop-in change.

payload.impact_rationale: Reusing hexgen's existing frozen verifier as a dense, per-command progress signal for RL fine-tuning directly targets two top-priority care areas at once (structural validity via execution-guided training, and verifier-in-the-loop / self-play training), and the paper shows a concrete completion-rate gain (+4.1pp) plus the key finding that credit must be assigned at the turn/command level rather than only at the end -- a specific, actionable design lesson for how hexgen would wire up such a reward.
payload.effort_rationale: Requires making a subset of the frozen verifier's checks meaningful on partial/incomplete programs and adding a GRPO-style RL fine-tuning stage on top of the current supervised-imitation training -- moderate new engineering, but it reuses the verifier hexgen already has rather than requiring a new model or dataset.
